es.summary: Acumulación excesiva de líquido en el parénquima cerebral que aumenta la presión intracraneal y compromete la perfusión neuronal.
key_points: Aumento de la presión intracraneal (PIC) > 20 mmHg es crítico.
Causas comunes: trauma, tumor, infección, hipoxia y síndrome de fuga de líquido cefalorraquídeo.
Manifiesta con cefalea, náuseas, vómitos y alteración del nivel de conciencia.
El diagnóstico se basa en neuroimagen (TC o RM) y evaluación clínica.
El manejo incluye control de la PIC, osmoterapia y medidas de soporte neurológico.

pathophysiology: Daño o inflamación rompe la barrera hematoencefálica.
Se produce extravasación de plasma al intersticio cerebral.
El aumento de volumen eleva la presión intracraneal.
La PIC alta reduce el flujo sanguíneo cerebral, provocando isquemia.
risk_factors: Meningitis, encefalitis y otras infecciones del SNC.
Síndrome de fuga de LCR tras cirugía o punción lumbar.
signs_symptoms: Náuseas y vómitos sin causa gastrointestinal.
Alteración del nivel de conciencia (confusión, somnolencia).
Rigidez de nuca y signos de herniación (pupila dilatada, bradicardia).
diagnostics: TC de cráneo: hipodensidad difusa, compresión ventricular.
RM cerebral: edema vasogénico o citotóxico, realce de la sustancia blanca.
Monitor de presión intracraneal (PIC) > 20 mmHg indica edema significativo.
Exámenes de laboratorio: glucosa, electrolitos, hemograma para descartar infección.
treatment: Elevación de la cabecera a 30°‑45° para favorecer drenaje venoso.
Osmoterapia con manitol o solución salina hipertónica (sin dosis específicas).
Ventilación controlada para mantener PaCO₂ 35‑40 mmHg (vasoconstricción cerebral).
Diuréticos como furosemida para controlar la sobrecarga de volumen.
Control de la fiebre y analgesia adecuada.
complications: Infección del sitio quirúrgico o catéter de ICP.
nursing_care: Evaluar nivel de conciencia cada hora usando la escala de Glasgow.
Monitorear PIC, presión arterial, frecuencia respiratoria y saturación O₂.
Mantener la cabecera elevada y evitar maniobras que aumenten la PIC.
Registrar tamaño y reactividad pupilar cada 2 h.
Controlar balance hídrico y signos de sobrecarga o deshidratación.
patient_teaching: Explicar la importancia de mantener la cabeza elevada y evitar tos o Valsalva.
Instruir sobre signos de alerta: empeoramiento de la cefalea, vómitos o cambios en la visión.
Enseñar la técnica de respiración profunda para evitar hipercapnia.
Informar sobre la necesidad de cumplir con estudios de imagen y controles de presión intracraneal.

en.summary: Excessive accumulation of fluid in the cerebral parenchyma that increases intracranial pressure and compromises neuronal perfusion.
key_points: Common causes: trauma, tumor, infection, hypoxia, and cerebrospinal fluid leak syndrome.
Manifested with headache, nausea, vomiting, and altered level of consciousness.
Diagnosis is based on neuroimaging (CT or MRI) and clinical assessment.
Management includes controlling ICP, osmotherapy, and neuro‑supportive measures.

pathophysiology: Damage or inflammation breaks the blood‑brain barrier.
Plasma extravasates into the cerebral interstitium.
High ICP reduces cerebral blood flow, causing ischemia.
risk_factors: Meningitis, encephalitis, and other CNS infections.
CSF leak syndrome after surgery or lumbar puncture.
signs_symptoms: Severe headache, worse when lying down.
Nausea and vomiting without gastrointestinal cause.
Nuchal rigidity and herniation signs (dilated pupil, bradycardia).
diagnostics: Head CT: diffuse hypodensity, ventricular compression.
Brain MRI: vasogenic or cytotoxic edema, white matter enhancement.
ICP monitor > 20 mmHg indicates significant edema.
Laboratory tests: glucose, electrolytes, CBC to rule out infection.
treatment: Elevate head of bed 30°‑45° to promote venous drainage.
Osmotherapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline solution (no specific dose).
Controlled ventilation to maintain PaCO₂ 35‑40 mmHg (cerebral vasoconstriction).
Diuretics such as furosemide to control volume overload.
complications: Surgical site or ICP catheter infection.
nursing_care: Assess level of consciousness hourly using the Glasgow Coma Scale.
Monitor ICP, blood pressure, respiratory rate, and O₂ saturation.
Keep head elevated and avoid maneuvers that increase ICP.
Record pupil size and reactivity every 2 h.
Track fluid balance and signs of overload or dehydration.
patient_teaching: Explain the importance of keeping the head elevated and avoiding coughing or Valsalva maneuvers.
Teach warning signs: worsening headache, vomiting, or vision changes.
Show deep breathing technique to avoid hypercapnia.
Inform about the need to comply with imaging studies and ICP checks.

care_plans.diagnosis: Risk for ineffective cerebral tissue perfusion

interventions.action: Elevate the bed head 30‑45° and maintain neutral neck position.
interventions.rationale: Facilitates venous drainage and reduces ICP.

interventions.action: Monitor ICP hourly and record values.
interventions.rationale: Detects early increases that require intervention.

interventions.action: Assess level of consciousness with the Glasgow Coma Scale every 30 min.
interventions.rationale: Changes in consciousness indicate deterioration of cerebral perfusion.

interventions.action: Administer osmotic agents (mannitol or hypertonic saline) as ordered.
interventions.rationale: Reduces intracranial volume via osmosis.

interventions.action: Maintain controlled ventilation for PaCO₂ 35‑40 mmHg.
interventions.rationale: Hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction and lowers ICP.

outcomes: Activity: patient will tolerate activities of daily living without increased fatigue within 48 h
Energy level: patient will report energy level ≥ 4/10 on Likert scale

interventions.action: Plan rest periods every 30‑45 min during light activities.
interventions.rationale: Prevents exhaustion and ICP elevation.

interventions.action: Assess intolerance signs (tachycardia, sweating, ICP rise) before and after activity.
interventions.rationale: Identifies safe effort limits.

interventions.action: Encourage relaxation and deep breathing techniques.
interventions.rationale: Reduces metabolic demand and helps maintain stable ICP.

interventions.action: Coordinate with physical therapy to initiate passive exercises and gradually progress.
interventions.rationale: Maintains mobility without overloading the nervous system.

interventions.action: Educate patient and family on the importance of rest and fatigue warning signs.
interventions.rationale: Promotes self‑management and early detection of deterioration.

key_points.2.quote: Patients with hemorrhagic strokes will more often complain of neck pain, photosensitivity, or nausea and vomiting; patients often present with subjective complaints of the worst headache of their life.

key_points.3.quote: Meningitis can be diagnosed through blood tests, lumbar puncture s of CSF, and imaging with CT scan s or MRI s.

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: meningioma — the most common type of benign intracranial tumor.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: Meningitis is an infection that causes inflammation in the brain and spinal cord.

sections.signs_symptoms.2.quote: If the infection progresses, patients may experience neurological symptoms, such as altered mental status, confusion, difficulty focusing, irritability, and seizure s.

sections.complications.1.quote: a lack of perfusion in an area of the brain can cause irreversible damage to the tissue in minutes.

sections.nursing_care.2.quote: Avoiding or minimizing bowel straining, coughing, or bearing down will reduce the risk of increases in ICP.

sections.nursing_care.4.quote: Monitor and maintain fluid and electrolyte balance.
